description: We're a group of friends from Córdoba, Argentina, who met up in Salta this week for a community event. We work in software and aerospace, and our team includes an aerospace engineer. Our project, Still There, is a 3D website for the Abandoned but not Forgotten challenge. It follows NASA machines from launch to where they rest today, on the Moon, Mars or deep space, using real NASA data.
summary: Still There web experience that tells the stories of 14 machines NASA left on the Moon, on Mars and in deep space. Each one is a mission you can fly through: the launch with its real rocket, the journey along its real JPL Horizons trajectory, and the machine today, with NASA photos, audio and video. It also includes an exploration mode and a mission-analyst game. Built only with NASA data and models, with every fact sourced, it turns discarded hardware into stories young people can explore and remember.
details:
What it does: Still There is a free 3D web app that tells the stories of 14 machines NASA left on the Moon, on Mars and in deep space. Each machine is a mission in chapters: the launch on its real rocket, including what happened to each discarded stage; the journey along its real JPL Horizons trajectory, with a timeline that shows date, speed, distances and radio delay; and the arrival and landing. The last chapter shows where the machine rests today, where you can tap its parts, see NASA photos, hear real mission audio and watch the real launch video. An exploration mode places every machine in a continuous solar system with live distances. A mission-analyst game lets players decide what to do when something fails, based on problems real machines faced.

Benefits and impact: These machines made history and are still out there, but their stories are scattered across archives and rarely reach young people. Still There makes them easy to explore and remember. It runs in any browser with no installation, works in English and Spanish, and can play a mission on its own for classrooms or museums.

Tools: JavaScript, HTML and CSS, with Three.js for 3D graphics, Python scripts to process the data and build the site, and GitHub Pages for hosting. Data comes from official NASA 3D models, JPL Horizons, NSSDCA, LROC and HiRISE imagery, and NASA press kits, photos, audio and video. AI assistants (Claude and Devin) helped with code and fact-checking. No visual, audio, video or 3D content was generated by AI.

Creativity: Instead of showing "abandoned hardware" as a static list, we turned each machine into a journey you live from launch to today. We also added a game that puts you in the role of the mission team.

Factors we considered: Scientific accuracy, which is why every fact has a source and anything illustrative is labeled on screen. We also considered accessibility for young audiences, performance on ordinary computers, open licenses (the project is Apache 2.0), and respect for NASA's media guidelines
dataRefs: NASA Space Science Data Coordinated Archive (NSSDCA)
